# Diagnosing ACC Power Loss on a Nissan Murano

When the dashboard remains completely dark in the Accessory (ACC) position while the radio and windows still function, you are dealing with a specific power distribution failure rather than a total system collapse. The fact that your 2005 Nissan Murano SL cranks, starts, and operates major systems like the windshield wipers and window motors indicates that the main battery feed to the starter solenoid and the primary ignition coil circuit is intact. However, the loss of all low-power accessoriesâinterior lights, dome light, map lights, rear wiper, and the key warning chimeâpoints directly to a failure in the accessory power rail or its control logic.

The most critical observation here is the sequence of events surrounding the battery replacement. You jumped the old battery to verify it was dead, then installed a new unit, after which the symptoms appeared. While you confirmed correct jumper cable order for the jump-start, there is a high probability that the new battery introduced a voltage spike or that the terminals were subjected to reverse polarity stress during the swap. This can damage sensitive Electronic Control Units (ECUs) or blow fuses designed to protect low-voltage subsystems.

Before diving into the difficult-to-access rear fuse box shown in your photo, it is essential to verify the front fuse panel under the dashboard. The symptoms describe a total loss of "ACC" power. In many Nissan models of this era, the ACC circuit is protected by a specific fuse that powers the instrument cluster backlighting and interior lamps. If this fuse blew during the jump-start or terminal connection, you would see exactly what you described: the radio (which often has a dedicated constant power feed or a separate relay) works, but the lighting circuits fail.

Check the rear fuse box for relays related to the "Interior Light" or "Wiper" functions. The rear windshield wiper is often on a separate circuit from the front wipers; its failure alongside the interior lights suggests they might share a common power source or relay. If you locate a relay labeled "PWR," "ACC," or specifically for the "Rear Wiper" in that box, swap it with a known good one to rule out mechanical failure.

If the fuses show continuity and the relays appear functional, the issue may lie with the Body Control Module (BCM) or the ignition switch itself. The BCM acts as the brain for interior lighting and wipers. If the voltage spike from the battery swap damaged the BCM's internal power regulation, it could refuse to distribute ACC power even if the main battery is healthy. To test this, you can try disconnecting the negative battery terminal for 15 minutes to reset the BCM's memory, though this is a temporary fix if the hardware is damaged.

Another potential pitfall is the ignition switch. The fact that you must turn the key fully to the "ON" position to light up the dash suggests the mechanical switch might be failing internally, cutting power to the ACC terminals prematurely or not engaging them at all. However, given the cluster of interior lights and wipers failing simultaneously, a blown fuse in the rear box remains the most probable culprit.

Inspect the specific fuses in that rear panel corresponding to "Interior Lamp," "Rear Wiper," and "Instrument Panel." Use your multimeter on continuity mode; if a fuse reads open circuit, replace it with one of the exact same amperage rating. Never exceed the rated amperage, as doing so risks melting the surrounding wiring insulation or causing further electrical damage. If no fuses are blown, the path between the battery and the BCM's power input may be compromised by corrosion introduced during the terminal swap. Clean the terminals thoroughly with a wire brush before reconnecting to ensure a low-resistance connection.

If you have ruled out blown fuses and suspect a damaged ECU or ignition switch, professional diagnosis of the BCM inputs will be required. But start with the accessible fuse panel and verify that no protective devices have tripped during the battery replacement process.
